prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, enabling measurement of time and frequency at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: B014 is still the candidate I find strongest, and the opening ballots strengthen that view: it is the only entry ranked in the top four by all eight members, with two first places. The invention is specific and original. Magic-wavelength trapping cancels the light shift that would otherwise ruin an optical clock in a lattice, and this lets very many atoms be interrogated at once. Katori proposed it and realized the first strontium clocks, and Ye's group then drove the systematic control to roughly 10^-18. The result has been reproduced independently in several laboratories and species, and it feeds directly into a possible redefinition of the second, relativistic geodesy, tests of constant variation and dark-matter searches. The attribution is as clean as any on the list: two people, one concept-and-first-realization, one performance frontier. The physics is also fundamental in the way the Prize traditionally means it, since it is about what we can measure and how well, and the atomic-physics content (control of differential light shifts, narrow clock transitions, many-body effects in dense lattices) is demanding and elegant.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap with the 2005 prize to Hall and Haensch for the frequency comb and precision laser spectroscopy, and the ion-clock lineage recognized in 2012. A critic can say that the lattice clock is a refinement of a recognized program rather than a new discovery of nature, and that the prize would honour an accuracy race in which several groups (ion clocks, Yb and Sr lattices at other institutes) took part. There is also a genuine split between the concept (Katori) and the later performance leadership (Ye), and the SI redefinition has not yet happened, so some members may want to wait for it. I think these are real points but not decisive: the 2005 work supplied the comb that links optical frequencies to counting electronics, while the lattice clock is a different invention with its own physics, and the concept-versus-performance split is the normal pattern for an instrument prize.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the lattice clock fourth and names overlap with the 2005 frequency-comb prize as the main allocation issue, while putting the quantum spin Hall effect first.
responses.response: I take the overlap seriously but I would separate the two cases. The comb made optical clocks countable; it did not supply the idea of trapping many atoms in a lattice with a magic wavelength so that the light shift cancels. That is the lattice-clock contribution, and it is a distinct invention with distinct physics. I also do not agree that B016 is clearly ahead on timeliness. It has the same kind of overlap problem with the 2016 topological-phases prize, which several colleagues, including Olsson and Eriksson, raise themselves.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B014 first for the same reasons I do, and ranks the Cirac-Zoller-Blatt controlled-atoms entry (B008) second, preferring a trapped-ion core to a combined ion and lattice prize.
responses.response: We agree on B014 and I accept his argument that the clock stands on its own. Where I differ is on B008 as a second choice. As a compound entry it mixes the ion-trap gate proposal, ion experiments and neutral-atom simulation, and the 2012 prize already covered control of single trapped ions, so the novelty has to be argued carefully. I would rather put the lattice-simulation work (B022) forward as the atomic-physics alternative, since it has a clearer identity. I accept that this choice has an attribution problem of its own: Greiner and Jaksch are not both accommodated, which Kroll's cleaner Cirac-Zoller-Blatt trio avoids.

responses.point: Johansson ranks B016 first, seeing a complete theory-to-experiment chain that is very mature, and ranks B014 third.
responses.response: I agree B016 is mature and that Kane and Mele's Z2 classification is deep. I put it as my first alternative rather than my choice because the attribution is the weak point in his own account: the HgTe proposal by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang is outside the credited names, and Zhang is deceased, so the Molenkamp half of the prize rests on an incomplete story. B014 has no comparable gap. If the committee prefers a condensed-matter prize, I could support B016, but I do not think the evidence puts it clearly ahead of B014, which is also the broader consensus pick across the ballots.

responses.point: Pearce ranks the IceCube neutrino discovery first as a clear new observational window, with a mature diffuse-flux result, while noting the difficulty of splitting credit within a large collaboration.
responses.response: I ranked B021 fourth, so I do not dismiss it, and the diffuse flux is a real discovery of a new messenger. My reservation is the one he states himself: the three credited names are defensible rather than uniquely correct given AMANDA, Baikal and other precursors and a very large collaboration, and source-level evidence is still at moderate significance. B014 is a smaller community, but the credit is much more precisely assignable, and the result is reproduced in several independent laboratories rather than resting on one facility. I would keep B021 as a strong candidate for a later year rather than this one.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks conformal field theory first, as a foundational and overdue framework with entirely stable interpretation, and ranks B014 third.
responses.response: I agree about the depth and the long-term stability of the conformal field theory work, and I ranked it seventh partly for reasons he states himself: Belavin is omitted from the credited names, and the experimental tests are indirect. A prize that excludes one of the authors of the founding paper is a serious credit problem for the committee, and the lattice clock does not have that problem. I do not think the experimental-confirmation criterion is the main issue; the attribution is.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as sufficiently separate from the 2005 frequency-comb prize, which is the single point on which opinion in the ballots most clearly splits.
Whether the committee prefers to wait for the formal redefinition of the SI second before recognising the work.
The priority details between Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and parallel ideas, and the secondary claims of other lattice-clock groups, are recalled from general knowledge and not verified here.
Whether a second part (for example B016) should be added to the prize; the three-person limit makes this difficult since B014 already uses two names.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile with Katori or Ye. I am a theoretical atomic physicist, so I know this field and some of its community, but the documented connections in my profile (the Gothenburg group, L'Huillier and the Lund attosecond group, Keller's group at ETH Zurich, Schuch, Dahlstrom, Argenti, Indelicato) concern other topics and none of these people is a credited name on B014, B016 or B022. I would flag the nearness of my field to atomic-physics candidates such as B014, B022, B008 and B005, and would state it openly if the committee asks.
